facts.claim: Rome was founded, according to Roman tradition
facts.context: Tradition put the founding at 753 BC and credited it to Romulus. The date is legendary rather than documented, and there were villages on the hills before it.
facts.goDeeper: Romans numbered their years from that date: AUC, ab urbe condita, 'from the founding of the city'.

facts.claim: Romans threw out their last king and founded the Republic
facts.context: The overthrow of Tarquin the Proud is traditionally dated to 509 BC. Like the founding, the date is traditional and historians treat it with caution.
facts.goDeeper: The Republic ran for roughly 480 years before Augustus, nearly twice as long as the United States has existed so far.

facts.claim: Hannibal marched an army with elephants over the Alps into Italy
facts.context: He crossed in 218 BC at the start of the Second Punic War and beat Roman armies in Italy for the next fifteen years without ever taking the city.
facts.goDeeper: He set out with about 37 elephants. Almost none of them survived their first winter in Italy.

facts.claim: Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army and began a civil war
facts.context: In January 49 BC he led a legion across the small river marking the northern edge of Italy, which no general was permitted to do under arms.
facts.goDeeper: The Rubicon is a stream so minor that scholars argued for centuries about which watercourse it actually was.

facts.claim: Julius Caesar was assassinated
facts.context: A group of senators stabbed him in Rome on the Ides of March, March 15, in 44 BC.
facts.goDeeper: He had been made dictator for life about a month earlier. The plot was meant to save the Republic and it finished it off instead.

facts.claim: Augustus became the first Roman emperor
facts.context: The Senate handed Octavian the name Augustus in 27 BC, seventeen years after Caesar was killed. Historians date the empire from there.
facts.goDeeper: He never used the word emperor. His title was princeps, 'first citizen', and he kept every form of the Republic while holding all of its power.

facts.claim: The Great Fire burned through much of the city of Rome
facts.context: The fire started near the Circus Maximus in July AD 64 and burned for six days, damaging or flattening ten of the city's fourteen districts.
facts.goDeeper: Nero rebuilt with wider streets and brick, and took a large slice of the burnt centre for a palace with its own artificial lake.

facts.claim: The Colosseum opened in Rome
facts.context: Begun under Vespasian and finished under his son Titus, it opened in AD 80 with a hundred days of games.
facts.goDeeper: Its actual name was the Flavian Amphitheatre. 'Colosseum' came from the colossal bronze statue of Nero that stood beside it.

facts.claim: Work began on Hadrian's Wall across northern Britain
facts.context: Building started around AD 122 on the emperor Hadrian's orders and took roughly six years. The exact start year is an estimate.
facts.goDeeper: It ran 73 miles from coast to coast, and it was not the frontier for long: a second wall went up further north twenty years later.

facts.claim: Constantine's Edict of Milan made Christianity legal across the empire
facts.context: The agreement of AD 313 ended official persecution and granted freedom of worship to Christians and to everyone else.
facts.goDeeper: Christianity did not become the official religion of the empire until AD 380, under Theodosius, nearly seventy years later.

facts.claim: The Visigoths under Alaric sacked the city of Rome
facts.context: Rome was entered and looted over three days in August AD 410, the first time a foreign army had got inside the city in 800 years.
facts.goDeeper: Rome was not even the capital by then. The western emperor was sitting safely behind the marshes at Ravenna while it happened.

facts.claim: The last emperor in the west was deposed, the traditional end of the Roman Empire
facts.context: Romulus Augustulus was pushed off the throne by the commander Odoacer in AD 476. The date is a convenient marker rather than a sudden collapse.
facts.goDeeper: The eastern half carried on from Constantinople for another thousand years, calling itself Roman the entire time.

source.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

facts.claim: Number of hills the city of Rome was built on
facts.context: Seven, traditionally: the Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine, Caelian, Esquiline, Quirinal and Viminal.
facts.goDeeper: The emperors lived on the Palatine, which is where the English word 'palace' comes from.

facts.claim: Soldiers in a Roman legion at full strength
facts.context: Roughly 5,000 men in ten cohorts. The figure moved about over the centuries and legions were very often under strength.
facts.goDeeper: A legionary signed on for 25 years and was paid off at the end with cash or a plot of land, which is close to the empire's version of a pension.

facts.claim: A vomitorium was a room where Roman diners went to throw up between courses
facts.context: A vomitorium is the passageway that lets a crowd pour out of an amphitheatre. The name is about spilling people into the street, not about vomiting.
facts.goDeeper: The banquet version is barely a century old, and it has outlived every attempt to correct it.

facts.claim: Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned
facts.context: The fiddle was not invented for another 1,400 years, and Tacitus records that Nero was at Antium, 30 miles away, when the fire broke out.
facts.goDeeper: Suetonius, writing fifty years later, says he sang about the fall of Troy. Tacitus reports the same story and calls it a rumour.

facts.claim: The caesarean section is named after the birth of Julius Caesar
facts.context: His mother Aurelia lived for decades afterwards, which the operation did not allow for at the time. The name most likely comes from the Latin caedere, to cut.
facts.goDeeper: Roman law did require the procedure in some cases, but as a burial rule rather than as surgery meant to save anyone.

facts.claim: Caesar's last words were 'Et tu, Brute?'
facts.context: That line is Shakespeare's. Suetonius reports that Caesar said nothing at the end, though some claimed he said in Greek, 'you too, child?'
facts.goDeeper: The play was written about 1,600 years after the event, and most of the popular picture of Caesar comes from it rather than from Rome.

facts.claim: Some Roman gladiators were free men who volunteered for the arena
facts.context: Most were enslaved or condemned, but free volunteers signed contracts for the pay and the fame, and a successful fighter could be released with a wooden sword.
facts.goDeeper: A star gladiator was a marketing property. His name went on oil lamps and cups the way an athlete's goes on a shoe today.

facts.claim: Most people in the city of Rome lived in rented apartment blocks
facts.context: The insulae were blocks of flats several storeys high with shops on the ground floor. Only the wealthy had a house to themselves.
facts.goDeeper: They were notorious for catching fire and for falling down, and Augustus capped their height at about 70 feet.
